analysis.one_liner: Gives student loan borrowers clear disclosures, fee limits, servicer accountability, and protections against abusive loan servicing.
analysis.headline: The Student Loan Borrower Bill of Rights never got a committee vote; it sat in the Senate education committee until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a "bill of rights" for people repaying student loans into the Truth in Lending Act. It would require lenders and servicers to warn borrowers before payments come due and before a loan is sent to collections, review borrowers for cheaper repayment plans when they fall behind, cap late fees, apply extra payments to the highest-interest loan, give borrowers a way to fix servicing errors, ban forced arbitration, and give servicemembers and veterans a specially trained contact and protection from default reporting while deployed. It would also let federal borrowers switch to a different servicer and create one central website for repaying federal loans [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly all student loan borrowers — private and federal — gain clearer information and fewer surprise fees. The biggest gains go to borrowers in distress: people who fall behind would get warnings before their loan is charged off, a 30-day window to apply for an affordable repayment plan, a single point of contact at the servicer, and a path to rehabilitate a charged-off private loan and clean up their credit [S2] [S3]. Servicemembers and veterans would get a specially trained liaison, a toll-free line, and a ban on having a loan charged off or reported delinquent while serving in a combat zone [S2] [S3]. Borrowers with multiple loans would benefit from rules requiring extra payments to go to the highest-interest balance first, and from limits on late fees — no fee within 15 days of the due date, none above 4% of the past-due amount, none per-loan in a billing group, and none when the servicer itself changes its payment-handling procedures [S2] [S3]. Borrowers could no longer be forced into pre-dispute arbitration, could get free copies of their original loan documents, and could get help applying for federal loan discharge they may be entitled to [S2] [S3]. Federal borrowers would gain the right to switch away from a bad servicer via random reassignment and a single centralized portal for all repayment [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student loan borrowers, especially distressed ones and servicemembers

how_it_helps.text: Requires lenders to disclose loan terms, the first payment date, and alternative repayment plans at least 30 days before the first fully amortized payment is due, and to warn borrowers 30 days delinquent about when the loan will be charged off or sent to collections and exactly what payment would avoid that

When a borrower is 60 days delinquent or says they are struggling, the lender must review the loan, tell the borrower which alternative repayment plans or servicemember and veteran benefits they qualify for, and give them at least 30 days to apply

Caps late fees — none above 4% of the past-due payment, none before 15 days past the due date, none more than once per late payment, none per-loan when loans are in a billing group, and none when a late payment is caused by the servicer's own change of address or payment procedures
Requires servicers, unless the borrower directs otherwise, to apply payments and extra payments to the loan with the highest interest rate first, and to post payments on the day they are received

Gives distressed borrowers a single point of contact at the servicer, a written response to account disputes within 5 business days and resolution within 30, protection from negative credit reporting during a dispute, and free access to their full loan history and original loan documents
Bans pre-dispute arbitration clauses and waiver of borrowers' rights, making servicers suable in court for violations

Creates a Servicemember and Veterans Liaison at every servicer with a toll-free line, and prohibits charging off or reporting as delinquent or in default any loan held by a servicemember on active duty in a combat zone

Lets a private loan be 'rehabilitated' — with the delinquency and charge-off removed from the borrower's credit history — after 9 on-time-ish payments over 10 consecutive months, or if the borrower otherwise brings the loan current after a charge-off

Requires the CFPB to write rules so lenders and servicers identify and contact borrowers who may be eligible to have their loans discharged by the Education Department and give them a streamlined application process

Before certifying a private loan, colleges must confirm the student has exhausted federal aid options, and the school may not certify any private loan that lacks alternative repayment plans or cancels the debt on death or disability of the borrower

Bars servicers from using servicing data to market other financial products to student borrowers, lets federal borrowers switch to a new servicer by random reassignment, and requires a centralized point of access and payment processing for all federal loans in repayment

analysis.who_pays: Student loan lenders and servicers pay. They would bear the cost of new disclosure and compliance systems, CFPB rulemaking requirements, annual reporting, error-resolution and dispute-response staff, trained servicemember liaisons, and a ban on marketing other products using servicing data [S2] [S3]. They would also lose revenue: capped and waived late fees, the requirement to apply payments in the borrower's favor (which shortens loans and cuts interest), a credit-repair pathway that erases charge-offs, and the loss of forced arbitration as a shield against borrower lawsuits [S2] [S3]. Colleges would take on new duties to verify federal aid is exhausted before certifying a private loan and could refuse certification of loans without borrower-friendly terms [S2] [S3]. Some of these costs could be passed back to borrowers as higher prices or tighter lending, and consumers who pay on time would see little direct benefit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Student loan servicers, private lenders, and colleges

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden on lenders and servicers is heavy — new disclosures, trained liaisons, dispute-response deadlines, error-resolution systems, annual CFPB reporting — and some of that cost could be passed to borrowers through higher prices or tighter credit

The bill contains a significant loophole: a lender may issue a private loan with no school certification at all if the college simply fails to respond within 15 business days, which weakens the very 'know before you owe' guardrail the bill is meant to strengthen
The servicer-switch program works by random reassignment, so a borrower unhappy with one servicer cannot choose a better one — they take whatever the Education Department deals them
Because it was never marked up or debated in committee, there is no record of how the provisions would have been refined, costed, or amended in practice

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete for the borrowers who need help most — the ones already behind, facing collections, or serving in the military — and the main costs fall on servicers and lenders in the form of compliance spending and lost fee and interest revenue, some of which might be passed on to borrowers. The design has real flaws, notably the 15-business-day loophole that lets private loans bypass school certification and the randomness of the servicer-switch program. On balance, the protections for distressed borrowers and servicemembers outweigh the costs, and the strongest critique is not that the bill was bad policy but that it never got the committee scrutiny that could have fixed its loopholes.

outcome.mechanism: Durbin introduced it in March 2015 and the Senate's education committee never took it up, so it died quietly when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin, joined by original cosponsors Senators Reed and Warren, introduced the bill on March 23, 2015
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the full Senate never considered it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan servicers and private lenders came out ahead: they avoided the disclosure, fee, payment-application, arbitration, and marketing rules the bill would have imposed. Borrowers — particularly distressed borrowers and servicemembers — got none of the protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student loan servicers and private lenders

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Student Loan Borrower Bill of Rights in the Senate

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup and never voted on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the 114th Congress

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded; the only on-record support was three Democrats (Durbin, Reed, Warren), and the Republican-run Senate education committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: Servicers would face binding rules on how they apply payments, when they can charge late fees, how fast they must answer disputes, and a ban on selling borrowers other products using servicing data — plus loss of forced arbitration as a defense. Servicer revenue historically depends on fees, steering distressed borrowers into forbearance, and cross-marketing, all of which the bill targets.

industries.industry: Private student lenders and loan investors
industries.note: Lenders would face new disclosure duties before repayment and before collections, mandatory alternative repayment plans and death/disability discharge as a condition of school certification, and a credit-rehabilitation pathway that erases charge-offs from borrowers' records. Loans could also no longer be sold or transferred without 45-day notice and a 60-day window protecting borrowers from late fees during the switch.

industries.industry: Debt collectors and credit reporting agencies
industries.note: Clear pre-collection warnings, a 30-day window to enroll in a repayment plan, combat-zone reporting protections, and mandatory removal of charge-offs after rehabilitation would reduce the volume of defaulted loans flowing to collectors and the negative information reported to credit bureaus.

Schools would have to certify private loan amounts against the student's remaining need and verify federal aid was exhausted first, and could refuse to certify loans lacking repayment plans or death/disability discharge. A 15-business-day response deadline, after which lenders can issue loans anyway, limits how much the certification requirement can actually block a loan.
